'I truly cook not badly.' The phrasing opens with 'really' before bringing in 'not bad' and 'prepare' to make the point clear.
'Yes, I know that perfectly well.' Kristina expresses this naturally by combining the word for 'perfectly' with 'know'.
'These are very tasty rolls.' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be' here, linking 'very much' directly with 'tasty', combining 'very much' with 'tasty' and 'sushi roll'.
'Did you prepare them yourself?' Kristina uses the informal singular 'you' here with 'myself', as friends and close colleagues do.
'Yes, specially for you.' Chef Barinov delivers a punchy one-word reaction built around the Russian word meaning 'on purpose'.
'They look very appetizing.' Kristina chooses the imperfective verb meaning 'to look' for the ongoing action, followed by 'very much' and 'appetizingly'.

'Yes, with great pleasure.' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be' here, linking 'great' directly with 'pleasure', combining 'great' with 'pleasure'.
'I am sure you will like it very much.' Notice the reflexive ending on the verb for 'will please', which directs the action back onto the subject.
'Your food is always the best.' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be', connecting 'your' directly with 'best'. Now let's listen to the whole conversation again from start to finish.

Kristina is genuinely impressed by the delicious food, proving that the chef's talent can solve almost any problem. Next time you watch the episode, listen for the Russian expressions for 'to know' and 'thing' — you will catch every word right away. See you in the next scene.
